note: Second half of the inference is reversed: source says whoever desires nothing lacks nothing.
replacement: No, replied Socrates, consider whether 'necessarily' is not the better word. In my judgment, Agathon, it is absolutely and necessarily true that whoever desires something lacks it, and that whoever desires nothing lacks nothing. What do you think?

note: "surely" dropped from "Love is surely admitted by all".
replacement: 'Right opinion,' she replied. 'As you know, it cannot give a reason, so it is not knowledge (for how can knowledge be without reason?). Nor is it ignorance (for ignorance cannot reach the truth). It is clearly something in between ignorance and wisdom.' 'Quite true,' I replied. 'Then do not insist,' she said, 'that whatever is not beautiful is necessarily ugly, or that whatever is not good is evil. And do not conclude that because love is not beautiful and good he must be ugly and evil. He is in between them.' 'Well,' I said, 'surely everyone admits that Love is a great god.' 'Everyone who knows, or everyone who does not know?' 'Everyone.' 'And how, Socrates,' she said with a smile, 'can Love be acknowledged a great god by those who say he is not a god at all?' 'And who are they?' I said. 'You and I are two of them,' she replied. 'How can that be?' I said. 'It is quite easy to understand,' she replied. 'You yourself would admit that the gods are happy and beautiful. Of course you would. Would you dare to say that any god was not?' 'Certainly not,' I replied. 'And by the happy you mean those who possess good and beautiful things?' 'Yes.' 'And you admitted that Love, because he lacks them, desires the good and beautiful things that he lacks?' 'Yes, I did.' 'But how can he be a god if he has no share in what is good or beautiful?' 'He cannot.' 'Then you see that you too deny that Love is divine.'

note: "thou stranger woman" (a stranger/foreigner) rendered as "strange woman"; keep vocative "stranger woman".
replacement: I said, 'You, stranger woman, speak well. But if Love is as you say, what use is he to men?' 'That, Socrates,' she replied, 'I will try to explain. I have already told you of his nature and birth, and you agree that love is of the beautiful. But someone will ask: of the beautiful in what, Socrates and Diotima? Or rather, let me put the question more clearly: when a man loves the beautiful, what does he desire?' I answered her, 'That the beautiful may be his.' 'Still,' she said, 'your answer raises another question: what does a man get by having beauty?' 'I have no answer ready for what you ask,' I replied. 'Then,' she said, 'let me put the word "good" in place of the beautiful and ask again: if he who loves loves the good, what is it that he loves?' 'The possession of the good,' I said. 'And what does he gain who possesses the good?' 'Happiness,' I replied. 'That is easier to answer.' 'Yes,' she said, 'the happy are made happy by acquiring good things. And there is no need to ask why a man desires happiness. The answer is already final.' 'You are right,' I said.

note: "conceive or contain" changed to "conceive and bring forth"; "contain" is lost.
replacement: 'Those who are pregnant in the body only turn to women and beget children. This is the character of their love. They hope that their offspring will preserve their memory and give them the blessedness and immortality that they desire for the future. But there are those who are pregnant in soul, for certainly there are men who are more creative in their souls than in their bodies. They conceive what is proper for the soul to conceive or contain. And what are these conceptions? Wisdom and virtue in general. Such creators are the poets and all artists who deserve the name of inventor. But by far the greatest and most beautiful kind of wisdom is the kind concerned with the ordering of states and families, which is called temperance and justice. And when someone has had the seed of these implanted in him from youth, and is himself inspired, he desires on reaching maturity to beget and bring forth.

note: "married by a far nearer tie" lost the marriage figure ("bound").
replacement: He wanders about looking for beauty in which he may beget offspring, for in ugliness he will beget nothing. Naturally he embraces beautiful bodies rather than ugly ones. Above all, when he finds a beautiful and noble and well-nurtured soul, he embraces both in one person. To such a person he is full of talk about virtue, and about the nature and pursuits of a good man, and he tries to educate him. At the touch of the beautiful, which is always present to his memory even when the other is absent, he brings forth what he had conceived long before. Together they raise what he has brought forth. They are married by a far closer tie and a firmer friendship than those who beget mortal children, because the children they share are more beautiful and more immortal. Who, thinking of Homer and Hesiod and the other great poets, would not rather have their children than ordinary human ones? Who would not wish to rival them in producing children like theirs, which have preserved their memory and given them everlasting glory? Or who would not want children like those Lycurgus left behind him, the saviors, one may say, not only of Lacedaemon but of Hellas?
